## Executive Summary

## The Problem: A Converging Strategic and Environmental Threat

Low Earth Orbit (LEO) has become a contested domain where **national security postures and orbital environmental degradation are inseparable**. Since the dawn of the space age, the mass of inert debris has exceeded that of operational spacecraft; today, catalogued fragments from debris-generating anti-satellite (ASAT) tests alone number 6,904 objects, of which **2,773 remain in orbit** — a stark reminder of the permanence imposed on the orbital environment by kinetic counterspace warfare [7]. The 27 March 2019 Indian "Mission Shakti" test and the 2021 Russian Nudol intercept exemplify a resurgent willingness among nation-states to destroy orbital assets, despite the coalescence of global regulatory consensus embodied by the **2002 IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines** [33]. The current threat landscape is thus defined by a dangerous coupling: **the growth of counter- space arsenals and the exponential proliferation of megaconstellation satellites**, which together render the orbital commons vulnerable to a self-sustaining collision cascade.

## Key National Capabilities (2026)

As of 2026, four states possess demonstrated or highly probable kinetic ASAT capabilities, with the US and China additionally fielding advanced co-orbital and directed-energy options:

| Country | Kinetic System(s) | Co-Orbital / Other | Debris Contribution (catalogued on orbit from ASAT tests) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **USA** | SM-3 Block IIA (exo-atmospheric), F-15/ASM-135 (historical) | Ground-based lasers, cyber/EW, advanced SSA [7] | 0 (no ASAT test since 2008, partial debris decayed) |
